parts.text:
A curve $C$ has equation
$y = \dfrac{3}{(5-3x)^2}, \quad x \neq \dfrac{5}{3}$
The point $P$ on $C$ has $x$-coordinate 2. Find an equation of the normal to $C$ at $P$ in the form $ax+by+c=0$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
At $P$, $y = \underline{3}$ B1
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3(-2)(5-3x)^{-3}(-3)$ $\left\{\text{or } \dfrac{18}{(5-3x)^3}\right\}$ M1A1
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{18}{(5-3(2))^3} \{=-18\}$ M1
$m(N) = \dfrac{-1}{-18}$ or $\dfrac{1}{18}$ M1
N: $y-3 = \dfrac{1}{18}(x-2)$ M1
N: $\underline{x-18y+52=0}$ A1
1st M1: $\pm k(5-3x)^{-3}$ can be implied. See appendix for application of the quotient rule.
2nd M1: Substituting $x=2$ into an equation involving their $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$;
3rd M1: Uses $m(N) = -\dfrac{1}{\text{their }m(T)}$.
4th M1: $y-y_1=m(x-2)$ with 'their NORMAL gradient' or a "changed" tangent gradient and their $y_1$. Or uses a complete method to express the equation of the tangent in the form $y=mx+c$ with 'their NORMAL ("changed" numerical) gradient', their $y_1$ and $x=2$.
Note: To gain the final A1 mark all the previous 6 marks in this question need to be earned. Also there must be a completely correct solution given.

questions.stem:
The function f is defined by
$\mathrm{f}: x \mapsto |2x-5|, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Sketch the graph with equation $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$, showing the coordinates of the points where the graph cuts or meets the axes.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: V or graph with vertex on the $x$-axis.
A1: $\left(\dfrac{5}{2},\{0\}\right)$ and $(\{0\},5)$ seen and the graph appears in both the first and second quadrants.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Solve $\mathrm{f}(x)=15+x$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $x=20$ B1
$2x-5=-(15+x); \Rightarrow \underline{x=-\dfrac{10}{3}}$ M1;A1 oe.
M1: Either $2x-5=-(15+x)$ or $-(2x-5)=15+x$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The function g is defined by
$\mathrm{g}: x \mapsto x^2-4x+1, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}, \quad 0\leqslant x \leqslant 5$
(c) Find $\mathrm{fg}(2)$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\mathrm{fg}(2) = \mathrm{f}(-3) = |2(-3)-5|; = |-11| = 11$ M1;A1
M1: Full method of inserting $\mathrm{g}(2)$ into $\mathrm{f}(x)=|2x-5|$ or for inserting $x=2$ into $|2(x^2-4x+1)-5|$. There must be evidence of the modulus being applied.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Find the range of g.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $\mathrm{g}(x) = x^2-4x+1 = (x-2)^2-4+1 = (x-2)^2-3$. Hence $\mathrm{g}_{min}=-3$ M1
Either $\mathrm{g}_{min}=-3$ or $\mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant -3$ or $\mathrm{g}(5)=25-20+1=6$ B1
$\underline{-3\leqslant \mathrm{g}(x)\leqslant 6}$ or $-3\leqslant y \leqslant 6$ A1
M1: Full method to establish the minimum of g. Eg: $(x\pm\alpha)^2\pm\beta$ leading to $\mathrm{g}_{min}=\beta$. Or for candidate to differentiate the quadratic, set the result equal to zero, find $x$ and insert this value of $x$ back into $\mathrm{f}(x)$ in order to find the minimum.
B1: For either finding the correct minimum value of g (can be implied by $\mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant -3$ or $\mathrm{g}(x)>-3$) or for stating that $\mathrm{g}(5)=6$.
A1: $-3\leqslant \mathrm{g}(x)\leqslant 6$ or $-3\leqslant y\leqslant 6$ or $-3\leqslant \mathrm{g}\leqslant 6$. Note that: $-3\leqslant x \leqslant 6$ is A0.
Note that: $-3\leqslant \mathrm{f}(x)\leqslant 6$ is A0. Note that: $-3\geqslant \mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant 6$ is A0.
Note that for the final Accuracy Mark: If a candidate writes down $-3<\mathrm{g}(x)<6$ or $-3<y<6$, then award M1B1A0. If, however, a candidate writes down $\mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant -3$, $\mathrm{g}(x)\leqslant 6$, then award A0. If a candidate writes down $\mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant -3$ or $\mathrm{g}(x)\leqslant 6$, then award A0.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Note that: $\mathrm{g}(x)\geqslant -3$ or $\mathrm{g}(x)>-3$ or $x\geqslant -3$ or $x>-3$ with no working gains M1B1A0.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows a sketch of the curve $C$ with the equation $y=(2x^2-5x+2)\mathrm{e}^{-x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the coordinates of the point where $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) Either $y=2$ or $(0,2)$ B1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Show that $C$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=2$ and find the $x$-coordinate of the other point where $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) When $x=2$, $y=(8-10+2)\mathrm{e}^{-2}=0\mathrm{e}^{-2}=0$ B1
$(2x^2-5x+2)=0 \Rightarrow (x-2)(2x-1)=0$ M1
Either $x=2$ (for possibly B1 above) or $\underline{x=\dfrac{1}{2}}$. A1
If the candidate believes that $\mathrm{e}^{-x}=0$ solves to $x=0$ or gives an extra solution of $x=0$, then withhold the final accuracy mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (4x-5)\mathrm{e}^{-x} - (2x^2-5x+2)\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ M1A1A1
M1: (their $u'$)$\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ + $(2x^2-5x+2)$(their $v'$)
A1: Any one term correct.
A1: Both terms correct.

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Hence find the exact coordinates of the turning points of $C$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $(4x-5)\mathrm{e}^{-x} - (2x^2-5x+2)\mathrm{e}^{-x} = 0$ M1
$2x^2-9x+7=0 \Rightarrow (2x-7)(x-1)=0$ M1
$x=\dfrac{7}{2}, 1$ A1

1st M1: For setting their $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ found in part (c) equal to 0.

(4)

parts.text:

(c) Calculate the maximum value of $H$ predicted by this model and the value of $t$, to 2 decimal places, when this maximum occurs.
(3)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Simplify fully
$\dfrac{2x^2+9x-5}{x^2+2x-15}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\dfrac{(x+5)(2x-1)}{(x+5)(x-3)} = \dfrac{(2x-1)}{(x-3)}$ M1 B1 A1 aef
M1: An attempt to factorise the numerator.
B1: Correct factorisation of denominator to give $(x+5)(x-3)$. Can be seen anywhere.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that
$\ln(2x^2+9x-5)=1+\ln(x^2+2x-15), \quad x\neq -5,$
(b) find $x$ in terms of e.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\ln\left(\dfrac{2x^2+9x-5}{x^2+2x-15}\right)=1$ M1
$\dfrac{2x^2+9x-5}{x^2+2x-15}=\mathrm{e}$ dM1
$\dfrac{2x-1}{x-3}=\mathrm{e} \Rightarrow 3\mathrm{e}-1=x(\mathrm{e}-2)$ M1
$\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3\mathrm{e}-1}{\mathrm{e}-2}$ A1 aef cso
M1: Uses a correct law of logarithms to combine at least two terms. This usually is achieved by the subtraction law of logarithms to give $\ln\left(\dfrac{2x^2+9x-5}{x^2+2x-15}\right)=1$. The product law of logarithms can be used to achieve $\ln(2x^2+9x-5)=\ln(\mathrm{e}(x^2+2x-15))$. The product and quotient law could also be used to achieve $\ln\left(\dfrac{2x^2+9x-5}{\mathrm{e}(x^2+2x-15)}\right)=0$.
dM1: Removing ln's correctly by the realisation that the anti-ln of 1 is e. Note that this mark is dependent on the previous method mark being awarded.
M1: Collect $x$ terms together and factorise. Note that this is not a dependent method mark.
A1: $\dfrac{3\mathrm{e}-1}{\mathrm{e}-2}$ or $\dfrac{3\mathrm{e}^1-1}{\mathrm{e}^1-2}$ or $\dfrac{1-3\mathrm{e}}{2-\mathrm{e}}$. aef
Note that the answer needs to be in terms of e. The decimal answer is 9.9610559...
Note that the solution must be in order for you to award this final accuracy mark.
Note: See Appendix for an alternative method of long division.
